segments.title: The choice between gun caliber and speed was political as well as technical
segments.body: The Royal Navy already depended on thirteen major ships armed with 15-inch guns and needed fast capital ships able to move around a global empire. A new 15-inch/50 weapon could support fleet standardization while freeing weight for machinery. In this interpretation, Nelson's slow, heavily protected design reflected political attraction to an apparently unsinkable centerpiece of the battle line. Political choices provide the counterfactual's starting point because they involve judgments that could have gone another way. Britain could have presented a smaller-caliber design as a gesture of confidence in naval arms limitation while gaining useful speed. The scenario is most persuasive through design, construction, and the first London treaty, since later events introduce too many interacting changes.

evidence.note: Political motives for 16-inch battleships, the case for standardized guns and speed, and the limits of projecting the counterfactual beyond the first London treaty.

segments.summary: Britain could plausibly have traded 16-inch guns for speed, presenting the choice as both an imperial requirement and a gesture of confidence in naval arms limitation.

segments.title: The Washington treaty permitted two British capital ships without requiring 16-inch guns
segments.body: The Washington treaty allowed Britain to construct two capital ships of no more than 35,000 tons standard displacement, with four older ships to be disposed of on their completion. Britain and the United States each received 525,000 tons of capital-ship replacement tonnage, Japan 315,000, and France and Italy 175,000 each. The British allocation covered the empire, preventing transfers to dominion fleets from providing an escape from the overall limit. The 35,000-ton displacement and 16-inch gun caliber were ceilings, leaving room for different combinations of protection, armament, and speed. Britain could therefore choose 15-inch guns if naval requirements outweighed the prestige of matching American and Japanese 16-inch ships.

evidence.note: Articles 2 through 6: British construction and disposal provisions, national tonnage allocations, and displacement and gun-caliber ceilings.

segments.summary: The treaty authorized Britain to build two 35,000-ton capital ships and capped guns at 16 inches, leaving room for a smaller-caliber fast design.

segments.title: An improved 15-inch gun might fit the treaty's reconstruction wording
segments.body: The reconstruction rules prohibited changes to the caliber, number, or general mounting type of retained ships' main armament. An improved 15-inch gun would retain the caliber and could use an existing turret with modified machinery. Contemporary legal and industrial arguments reportedly explored this reading separately from the F2 and F3 design debate, although it strained the treaty's spirit. Increasing turret elevation offered another possible improvement. Installing the heavier barrels would require balancing and mechanical changes, making peacetime refits a suitable opportunity. Slow, space-intensive conversion work could keep specialist industrial infrastructure open without requiring a wartime-sized workforce.

evidence.note: Reconstruction restrictions, the same-caliber and same-mounting argument, turret modifications, and the industrial value of peacetime refits.

segments.summary: A 15-inch/50 gun could arguably preserve caliber and mounting type while upgrading the Royal Navy's common battleship weapon.

segments.title: A common 15-inch barrel pool could support the longer gun's maintenance
segments.body: Replacing 15-inch/42 guns with 15-inch/50s during refits would retain the same shells while increasing barrel wear. More spare barrels and more frequent relining would therefore be necessary. The proposed fifteen-ship 15-inch fleet would comprise two nine-gun ships, eleven eight-gun ships, and two six-gun ships. A fleet that large would already require substantial barrel stocks, with a suggested reserve of roughly one barrel for every two mounted aboard ships. Standardizing the upgrade across the fleet could make the maintenance burden manageable while giving the guns performance closer to contemporary 16-inch weapons.

evidence.note: Gradual gun replacement, common shells, increased wear and relining, the proposed fleet's batteries, and the approximate reserve-barrel ratio.

segments.summary: More powerful 15-inch guns would need more frequent relining, but a large standardized fleet could share ammunition and reserve barrels.

segments.title: Subdivision and armor coverage separate battlecruisers from battleships
segments.body: Interwar capital-ship classification depended on more than speed or maximum belt thickness. Internal subdivision and the proportion of the hull protected by armor also help distinguish a dreadnought battleship, fast battleship, or battlecruiser. A battlecruiser might carry thicker armor over its vital area than a battleship while protecting less of the hull and providing less subdivision behind it. Fast battleships and battlecruisers also needed sufficient speed to maintain contact with the cruiser line. Comparing belt thickness alone therefore misses differences in hull construction and intended fighting role.

evidence.note: Hull subdivision, armor coverage and thickness, and the speed needed to maintain contact with the cruiser line.

segments.summary: Hull subdivision and the extent of armor coverage help distinguish capital-ship types alongside speed and maximum armor thickness.

segments.title: F2 and F3 show how armament weight bought Nelson's missing speed
segments.body: The F2, F3, and Nelson concepts carried broadly comparable armor weights, while Nelson's hull was about 750 tons heavier because of its greater subdivision. Their protection was distributed differently: F3 had a uniform 12-inch belt, while Nelson had 14 inches over the magazines and 13 over the machinery. F3's armament weighed about 1,550 tons less, matching the increase from Nelson's 2,550-ton machinery plant to F3's 4,100-ton plant. That machinery raised the proposed output from 45,000 to 96,000 shaft horsepower and the speed from about 23 to 28.5 knots. F2 paired six 15-inch guns with 112,000 shaft horsepower for still greater speed. F2 and F3 remain battlecruisers in this classification because of their subdivision, despite armor coverage approaching that of a battleship.

evidence.note: Hull and armor weights, belt thicknesses, and the exchange of 1,550 tons of armament weight for F3's larger machinery plant.

segments.summary: Comparing weights and machinery suggests that substituting nine 15-inch guns for Nelson's 16-inch battery could fund roughly 28-knot performance without abandoning heavy protection.

segments.title: John Brown shaft engineering makes F3 power technically plausible
segments.body: F2, F3, and Nelson were all two-shaft designs, so F3's 96,000 shaft horsepower raises a metallurgy and transmission question. The proposed engineering connection is John Brown's work with Curtis on turbines and shaft design, which makes that power output appear technically plausible. Nelson's standard displacement sat below the 35,000-ton treaty ceiling, suggesting room to consider a faster battleship with adjusted protection. A designer might have needed a uniform 13-inch belt or other armor changes to accommodate more machinery. Such a ship could remain within the standard-displacement ceiling even while exceeding 35,000 tons fully loaded.

evidence.note: Two-shaft power transmission, the possible John Brown and Curtis engineering connection, and armor adjustments within the standard-displacement limit.

segments.summary: Contemporary British turbine and shaft development offers a possible basis for F3's high output; a faster battleship near the treaty limit might also require armor adjustments.

segments.title: F3 balanced nine heavy guns, 28.5-knot speed, and room for later upgrades
segments.body: F3 retained nine 15-inch guns while sacrificing four 6-inch secondary guns compared with F2, leaving deck space for later anti-aircraft weapons. Its 740-foot hull was longer than Nelson's 710 feet, though shorter than F2's 760 feet, with the beam held at 106 feet. Greater length at a constant beam could improve efficiency through the water, subject to hull shape and other design details. The main-battery arrangement also offered better forward firing arcs, with the advantages and risks of a more nearly bow-on approach. The layout appeared adaptable to an aft-facing aircraft catapult if independent operations created a need for aircraft.

evidence.note: Secondary-armament and deck-space differences, hull dimensions, forward firing arcs, and possible aircraft arrangements.

segments.summary: F3 retained nine 15-inch guns, used a longer hull than Nelson, and offered space for later anti-aircraft and aviation additions.

segments.title: F3's forward firing arcs change the risks of a bow-on approach
segments.body: F3's turret arrangement could allow a more nearly bow-on approach at long range, while Nelson would need to turn farther to clear the guns. Presenting a narrow target would make shells dispersed to either side more likely to miss. A shell falling along the ship's length could still hit and potentially cause considerable damage. The advantage is a reduced risk of multiple hits from a salvo, with a different exposure to individual shells. The preferred approach would depend on the engagement.

evidence.note: Forward firing arcs, bow-on target width, and the contrasting risks of lateral shell dispersion and lengthwise hits.

segments.summary: A narrow bow-on target could reduce hits from a dispersed salvo, while remaining vulnerable to shells falling along the ship's length.

segments.title: Independent operations strengthen the case for aircraft aboard F3
segments.body: F3's arrangement appears suitable for a later aircraft installation, including an aft-facing catapult. The proposed layout would launch the aircraft behind the ship instead of across it. Nelson and Rodney were expected to remain with other fleet units, reducing the perceived need for their own aircraft. Faster F3-derived ships would be more likely to operate separately, giving their own aircraft a stronger operational justification. The catapult remains a possible later alteration.

evidence.note: Possible aft-facing catapult and the connection between independent operations and an onboard aircraft requirement.

segments.summary: F3's likely independent deployments would give it a stronger reason to carry aircraft, with an aft-facing catapult among the proposed options.

segments.title: Perceptions of Jutland favored armor over strategic mobility
segments.body: In this interpretation, public and political imagery blamed insufficient armor for the battlecruiser losses while obscuring ammunition handling and command failures. That perception made an apparently unsinkable battleship with 16-inch guns attractive. Yet Royal Navy design work before and after the war repeatedly emphasized battlecruisers because speed supported imperial defense and power projection. Procurement institutions often have to respond to the perceived meaning of events rather than their more complicated operational causes.

evidence.note: Political perceptions of Jutland, ammunition handling and command failures, and the case for strategic mobility.

segments.summary: In this interpretation, political concern over Jutland's losses encouraged an armored centerpiece while the Royal Navy's wider commitments favored fast capital ships.

segments.title: F3 speed and common ammunition offered peacetime and wartime flexibility
segments.body: F3's nine-gun battery offered a stronger balance than F2's six guns for a small reduction in speed. Ordinary quoted speeds excluded forced draft: 30 knots is treated as attainable under forced draft, while 31-32 knots remains a constructor's estimate. Common 15-inch ammunition and industrial support could reduce the cost of introducing a separate heavy-gun system. A possible mid-1930s refit would replace the eight 6-inch guns with 4.5-inch dual-purpose armament, although the eventual battery size remains uncertain. The faster ships could undertake worldwide presence missions while remaining able to return when needed, reducing the dependence on Hood. That mobility would also help them choose the circumstances of an engagement with slower opponents.

evidence.note: Ordinary and forced-draft speed estimates, common heavy-gun support, a possible 4.5-inch dual-purpose refit, and the operational value of speed.

segments.summary: A fast Nelson and Rodney could standardize heavy-gun logistics, travel for presence missions, and accept more useful interwar modernization.

segments.title: A common 15-inch gun system could support coastal defenses
segments.body: A larger 15-inch/50 program could reduce the expense of maintaining a separate 16-inch gun and ammunition system. Older 15-inch/42 weapons could also serve coastal defenses if they could use the same shells. Possible destinations include Singapore, the Channel coast, Scapa Flow, and Gibraltar. Starting the Singapore program earlier might allow more work to be completed before the Great Depression. The savings argument assumes that money would remain available to the navy because its budget became more stable after the Geddes cuts. The stated 41.4 percent reduction in British defense spending helps explain the attraction of avoiding another heavy-gun support system.

evidence.note: Conditional reuse of older guns, named coastal-defense locations, Singapore's possible earlier timetable, and the budget assumptions behind standardization.

segments.summary: Standardized ammunition and reused guns could support coastal defenses, with an earlier Singapore program among the possible benefits.

segments.title: Speed controls the range, angle, and pace of an engagement
segments.body: Five extra knots would shorten imperial transits and shape a battle once contact was made. Against slower 16-inch battleships, an F3-derived Nelson could use speed to choose the engagement range and maneuver onto a favorable bearing. That freedom affects whether combat begins as well as its angle, timing, and pace, reducing the opponent's ability to exploit nominal gun superiority. That speed would give a ship with smaller-caliber guns more control over the fight.

evidence.note: An F3-derived ship's speed would let it choose the range, angle, timing, and pace of battle against slower ships armed with 16-inch guns.

segments.summary: An F3-derived ship's speed advantage would be tactical as well as strategic, letting it choose when and how to fight opponents with heavier guns.

segments.title: Carrier aviation was emerging, but not yet mature
segments.body: Projecting the aircraft carrier of 1945 backward into the 1920s overstates what interwar naval aviation could do. Carriers were clearly developing, but their air groups and practical operating capability had not yet reached wartime maturity. A state could not base current defense on a system expected to dominate only in the future; it had to fund security across several time horizons. In this scenario, F3-derived capital ships and carrier development complement each other.

evidence.note: Differences between interwar and 1945 carrier air groups, and the need to fund present as well as future defense capability.

segments.summary: The counterfactual keeps battleships and carriers because 1920s air groups could not yet provide the mature combat power seen at the end of the Second World War.

segments.title: Fast Nelsons would give Britain a sustainable six-ship mobile force
segments.body: Tiger could not receive 15-inch guns under the treaty, but she could join Hood, Renown, Repulse, and the two proposed fast Nelsons in a six-ship pool. A one-in-three cycle would place ships in long maintenance, working up or down, and operational service, leaving two available for deployment. Rotating imperial cruises could demonstrate British reach in regions without a permanently based battle fleet. Speed would allow this limited force to arrive rapidly and concentrate where needed. Sharing deployments across six ships would also reduce wear and make major modernizations easier to schedule. Insufficient deployable ships is one proposed explanation for Renown alone receiving a modernization to late-1930s standards, despite available yard capacity and funding from 1937.

evidence.note: Tiger, Hood, Renown, Repulse, Nelson, and Rodney are combined into a six-ship readiness and presence model.

segments.summary: Adding two 28-knot Nelsons to Hood, Tiger, Renown, and Repulse would allow regular deployments and refits without making any single fast ship indispensable.

segments.title: Fast capital ships and carriers could revive the Royal Navy's flying squadron
segments.body: Furious, Courageous, and Glorious could each operate with a pair of fast capital ships, matching interwar exercises that explored carrier-supported searches for surface raiders and responses to distant crises. Six fast capital ships would provide a pool large enough to assemble these groups more consistently through maintenance and deployment cycles. A revived flying squadron, reinforced by cruisers and destroyers, would concentrate scarce power while remaining available to reinforce the main fleets. Such a mobile reserve had precedents in the nineteenth-century Royal Navy. Regular combined deployments could also develop naval aviation experience and give carriers a more established place in the command structure.

evidence.note: Carrier and fast-capital-ship combinations for raider hunting, crisis response, and the revival of a mobile flying squadron.

segments.summary: Six fast capital ships and three fast carriers could support repeatable task groups for raider hunting, crisis response, and worldwide presence.

segments.title: A flying squadron could bring a carrier command appointment forward
segments.body: Regular deployments with fast capital ships could strengthen naval aviation's place within the fleet. A permanent flying squadron might require a Rear Admiral Aircraft Carriers by 1928, two years before the historical creation of the post under Admiral Henderson. The proposed structure places a vice admiral over the force, with rear admirals responsible for another capital-ship group and the carriers. Those officers could then lead separate groups combining one carrier with two fast capital ships. Particular ship pairings remain speculative, and mixed groups of 28-knot and 32-knot ships are another possibility.

evidence.note: Possible 1928 carrier command appointment, flag-officer responsibilities, and alternative combinations of carriers and fast capital ships.

segments.summary: A larger fast force could support an earlier carrier command post and regular groups of one carrier with two capital ships.

segments.title: Fast Nelsons would outmaneuver Japanese and American battle lines
segments.body: Japan's Nagato class approached 26.5 knots, so maintaining a substantial speed advantage could require F3 to use forced draft at the cost of greater machinery wear. Only the Kongos are considered fast enough to bring F3 to battle, with that encounter judged unfavorable to the Japanese ships. The United States' largely 21-knot battle line would struggle to control engagement range against the proposed British fast squadron. France and Italy would face a British mobile force comparable to their entire allowed capital-ship strength. Italian Andrea Doria-class reconstructions gained speed after losing a turret, but that improvement is judged insufficient against the British squadron. A larger British fast force would also reduce the relative importance of France's Dunkerques in an Anglo-French fleet, while encouraging Britain to consider faster Queen Elizabeth-class reconstructions.

evidence.note: Nagato's speed and F3's forced-draft wear, the expected Kongo matchup, and American, French, and Italian responses to a larger British fast force.

segments.summary: The F3 Nelsons' speed would leave most foreign battleships unable to force an engagement and could pressure rivals toward new construction or modernization.

segments.title: Fast Nelsons could redirect Queen Elizabeth-class reconstruction toward speed
segments.body: As Tiger aged out of service, the Royal Navy would have a strong reason to prevent its fast force from falling below strength. Warspite's historically extensive reconstruction offered the clearest opportunity to test a 28-knot Queen Elizabeth by fitting new turbines, retaining more boiler capacity, and accepting other weight trades. If the concept worked, the class might receive a more standardized speed-focused program instead of spending resources on a different mix of older battleships such as Royal Oak. The result would also reduce the relative importance of France's Dunkerques within an Anglo-French fast-capital-ship force.

evidence.note: Machinery, boilers, secondary armament, and fleet strength could justify rebuilding Warspite or the wider Queen Elizabeth class toward 28 knots.

segments.summary: Maintaining a six-ship flying squadron could make 28-knot Queen Elizabeth-class rebuilds more valuable than historically chosen modernization priorities.

segments.title: Visible fast ships could strengthen deterrence and challenge Italy's speed advantage
segments.body: A warship seen in port gives a foreign public or decision-maker a concrete image of a capability that would otherwise remain abstract. In this account, regular carrier visits illustrate how visible presence contributes to conventional deterrence. A touring British fast squadron could produce a similar effect. Italy's pursuit of speed as an advantage in the Mediterranean would also become less convincing against a larger British fast force. The pressure would increase further if Queen Elizabeth-class reconstructions joined that force at 28 knots.

evidence.note: Visible naval presence as a source of deterrence, and the challenge a larger British fast force would pose to Italian speed policy.

segments.summary: Regular visits by fast capital ships could make British naval power more tangible and weaken Italy's attempt to gain an advantage through speed.

segments.title: F3 machinery could bring fleet speed requirements forward
segments.body: Building F3 would give Britain experience with the machinery needed for faster capital ships. Its initial boilers would be only slightly higher in pressure than Nelson's, with much of the extra power coming from having more of them. Further advances in boiler pressure would depend on the money and time available for development. Once capital ships could sustain the higher speed, planners would need to reconsider the operating speeds of cruisers, destroyers, and carriers serving with them. In this scenario, those requirements could become central to fleet design roughly a decade earlier.

evidence.note: The limited initial boiler-pressure increase, additional boilers, investment constraints, and the effect of fast capital ships on other fleet units' speeds.

segments.summary: More powerful capital ships could force earlier attention to escort and carrier speeds, although major boiler advances would still require investment.

segments.title: A 1929 flying-squadron tour could influence the London treaty talks
segments.body: Using the historical commissioning dates of 1927 for Nelson and Rodney and 1928 for Courageous, a flying-squadron cruise around 1929-30 fits the proposed timeline. The force might attend the twenty-fifth anniversary of Tsushima, combining the memory of the former alliance with a display of British naval power. American assessments placed Hood's fighting value alongside that of a Colorado-class battleship, despite her much greater speed. F3 would be slower than Hood but more heavily protected, making it a more threatening combination of speed, armament, and ability to withstand hits. A world tour could therefore make the speed disparity more conspicuous before the London treaty negotiations.

evidence.note: Commissioning dates, a possible Tsushima anniversary visit, and the assessment of F3's protection and speed compared with Hood.

segments.summary: A world tour by Nelson, Rodney, and a carrier could display a force more dangerous than Hood and sharpen foreign demands at the 1930 negotiations.

segments.title: A Mediterranean base could send the flying squadron east or west
segments.body: The proposed flying squadron would probably operate from the Mediterranean, placing it centrally for deployments across the British Empire. It could move east or west as required. Courageous's Mediterranean Fleet service fits this proposed arrangement, while Furious could transfer from the Atlantic Fleet to join the fast force. Concentrating several carriers would also strengthen the case for an earlier Rear Admiral Aircraft Carriers appointment.

evidence.note: Mediterranean basing for eastward or westward deployments, a possible Furious transfer, and the connection with multi-carrier command.

segments.summary: Mediterranean basing would combine access to eastern and western deployments with a concentration of fast capital ships and carriers.

segments.title: The London treaty might answer the speed gap with scheduled capital-ship construction
segments.body: The counterfactual reaches a fork at the first London treaty: if rival navies are unconcerned by British speed, nothing need change. If they demand new ships to close the gap, construction would require either a negotiated allowance or the breakdown of the treaty system. One proposed bargain would permit Britain and the United States roughly five new capital ships each, Japan three, and France and Italy two each over a six-to-seven-year cycle. That timing reflects the tension between convenient building periods, twenty-year replacement, and the tonnage limits. Britain might continue with 15-inch guns because the saved armament weight bought speed and other capabilities. Construction beginning around 1930 would initially favor F3 derivatives and other contemporary designs, with later development increasingly difficult to predict. The possibility that controlled replacement could prolong arms limitation remains conditional on the powers accepting the bargain.

evidence.note: Conditional foreign demand for construction, the alternatives of treaty breakdown or negotiated allowances, replacement cycles, and the limits of predicting later designs.

segments.summary: If rival navies regarded the F3 Nelsons as intolerable, a negotiated building cycle could preserve arms control while allowing new fast capital ships.

segments.title: Two shafts favored efficiency, while four offered redundancy
segments.body: Designs begun in 1930 would probably inherit F3's all-forward arrangement and then improve its armor and machinery. Retaining two shafts could preserve hull and hydrodynamic advantages if the system worked. Four shafts would give greater redundancy because a casualty could leave several independent lines of propulsion available. Three shafts offered an awkward compromise because the centerline shaft tended to create problems, making propulsion layout a real design choice rather than an incidental detail.

evidence.note: F3-style all-forward layouts and the hydrodynamic, redundancy, and reliability tradeoffs of two-, three-, and four-shaft propulsion.

segments.summary: An F3-derived generation would force a choice between two-shaft hydrodynamic efficiency and four-shaft damage tolerance, while three shafts offered a troublesome compromise.

segments.title: Continuous batches could evolve F3 into a fast battleship
segments.body: An allowance beginning around 1930 would let British yards move from Nelson and Rodney into batches of modified F3 derivatives instead of entering a long capital-ship hiatus. Initial ships could retain the design's speed while using improving boiler power density to add hull subdivision and protection. Across successive batches, a fully armored battlecruiser could evolve into a true fast battleship without a clean-sheet restart. Keeping construction active would preserve the infrastructure and experience needed for later expansion.

evidence.note: Successive British F3 derivatives, with greater subdivision and protection made possible by improving boiler power density.

segments.summary: A building allowance beginning around 1930 could carry British yards through successive F3 derivatives until the fully armored battlecruiser evolved into a true fast battleship.

segments.title: Renewed battleship building would force a new carrier bargain
segments.body: Renewed capital-ship building would also raise pressure to expand carrier tonnage because Britain and the United States wanted more flight decks. A separate alternative would distinguish battleships and battlecruisers in the treaty quotas. The suggested totals are fifteen battleships and five battlecruisers each for Britain and the United States, nine and three for Japan, and six and two each for France and Italy. That arrangement could favor Britain: it would gain room for new battleships while the United States used its allowance to fill a fast-ship deficit. A general capital-ship building allowance is consequently favored within the scenario because separate categories would give the two navies different benefits.

evidence.note: Possible carrier-tonnage expansion, proposed national battleship and battlecruiser quotas, and their unequal construction benefits.

segments.summary: Britain and the United States would want more carrier tonnage, but separating battleships and battlecruisers into different quotas could distribute useful construction rights unevenly.

segments.title: Earlier treaty-power construction could encourage Soviet Project 21
segments.body: Battleship construction by the treaty powers in the early 1930s would create pressure on outsiders to respond. Soviet Project 21 is one of the studies Stalin might advance if other powers were visibly building. The proposed outcome is a fast but lightly armored vessel, with an F3-like layout among the possibilities. The joking nickname "Nelsonski" conveys the resemblance of the concept without establishing that its internal design would match Nelson. This remains a conditional extension of the earlier construction scenario.

evidence.note: Possible Soviet response to renewed treaty-power construction, Project 21, and the speculative fast but lightly protected design.

segments.summary: New battleships in the treaty navies could put pressure on Stalin to advance Soviet capital-ship studies, including Project 21.

segments.title: Continuous construction could leave Germany facing a younger Royal Navy
segments.body: An active capital-ship building program would be easier to expand than an industry restarted after a prolonged gap. Restarting from cold brings additional costs and practical difficulties that continuous work could avoid. Germany's renewed naval construction would then face a Royal Navy with modernized older ships and a larger group of new fast capital ships. In one continuation of the proposed building allowances, as many as eight ships built during the 1930s could be in service by 1939. Counting Hood and the two Nelsons, eleven of a fifteen-ship force would have been launched since the First World War. Those totals depend on later treaty arrangements and building decisions, as does the choice between retaining 15-inch guns and moving to 16-inch weapons.

evidence.note: Industrial restart costs, the German catch-up problem, and conditional estimates for the age and composition of the British capital-ship force in 1939.

segments.summary: Successive building batches could preserve British yard capacity and make German rearmament confront a much more modern capital-ship force.

segments.title: The final choice was 16-inch firepower or another 5.5 knots
segments.body: F3's machinery was about 1,550 tons heavier than Nelson's, while its armament was lighter by essentially the same amount. The practical choice was nine 16-inch guns and twelve 6-inch guns at about 23 knots versus nine 15-inch/50s and eight 6-inch guns at roughly 28.5 knots. The extra 5.5 knots are favored here for the strategic opportunities they would provide. The weights quantify the exchange, while the preference for speed depends on its expected strategic value.

evidence.note: The matching machinery and armament weight differences, the two battery combinations, and the stated preference for another 5.5 knots.

segments.summary: The 1,550-ton exchange between armament and machinery frames the judgment between Nelson's heavier battery and F3's additional speed.
